sections.content:
## What You'll Learn

By the end of this lesson you'll understand Make's module-based visual approach to automation and be able to call the Anthropic API directly from a Make scenario using the HTTP module.

## What is Make?

Make (formerly Integromat) is a visual automation platform at make.com. Like n8n and Zapier, it connects apps and services. What distinguishes Make:

- **Visual canvas** — circular nodes connected by lines, very visual
- **Module-based** — every step is a "module" you configure
- **Generous free tier** — 1,000 operations/month free (an operation = one module execution)
- **Cloud-only** — no self-hosting option (unlike n8n)
- **Scheduling** — scenarios run on a schedule you define

Make sits between Zapier (most polished) and n8n (most powerful) in terms of complexity. It's popular with marketers and operations teams because its visual interface makes complex data transformations very readable.

## Calling Claude from Make

Make has a built-in OpenAI module, but **no official Anthropic/Claude module**. This is not a showstopper — Make's HTTP module lets you call any REST API, including the Anthropic Messages API.

The HTTP module sends a raw HTTP request. For Claude, that means:
- URL: `https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages`
- Method: POST
- Headers: three required headers
- Body: JSON with your model, max_tokens, and messages array

This is more setup than a dedicated module, but it gives you full control over the request and works with any Anthropic model.

**Alternative approaches:** If you want less HTTP configuration, you can (1) use the OpenAI module pointed at a Claude-compatible proxy, or (2) use n8n's native Claude integration from lesson 10-2 instead. The concept this lesson teaches — calling an API via HTTP in a visual tool — applies everywhere.

## The HTTP Module Configuration

Here is the exact configuration you'll use to call Claude from Make's HTTP module:

**URL:** `https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages`

**Method:** POST

**Headers:**
- `x-api-key` → your Anthropic API key
- `anthropic-version` → `2023-06-01`
- `content-type` → `application/json`

**Body (Raw / JSON):**

The `{{your_input_from_previous_module}}` part is Make's dynamic variable syntax — you map data from a previous module (like a Google Sheets row or email body) into the prompt.

The response comes back as a JSON object. To extract Claude's text response, parse: `body > content > 0 > text`.

sections.title: Build a Make Scenario Calling the Anthropic API
sections.content:
You'll build a scenario that watches a Google Sheet for new rows, sends the row content to Claude via the HTTP module for processing, and emails you the result.

**Setup:**
1. Go to make.com and sign up for the free tier
2. Have your Anthropic API key from lesson 11-3 ready (if you haven't done Part 11 yet, use a placeholder and come back)
3. Create a new Google Sheet with two columns: `Topic` and `Status`

**Build the Scenario:**

**Step 1 — Add the Google Sheets module (trigger)**
1. Click **Create a new scenario**
2. Click the large `+` on the canvas
3. Search for **Google Sheets** → choose **Watch new rows**
4. Connect your Google account
5. Select your spreadsheet and sheet
6. Set "Maximum number of returned rows" to 1

**Step 2 — Add the HTTP module**
1. Click the `+` on the right of the Google Sheets module
2. Search for **HTTP** → choose **Make a request**
3. Configure:
   - URL: `https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages`
   - Method: POST
   - Headers (click Add item for each):
     - Name: `x-api-key` / Value: `sk-ant-your-key-here`
     - Name: `anthropic-version` / Value: `2023-06-01`
     - Name: `content-type` / Value: `application/json`
   - Body type: Raw
   - Content type: JSON (application/json)
   - Request content (paste and replace the topic variable):
```
{"model":"claude-haiku-4-5-20251001","max_tokens":200,"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Write a 3-sentence social media post about this topic: {{1.Topic}}"}]}
```
   - Parse response: Yes

**Step 3 — Add the Gmail module**
1. Click `+` after the HTTP module
2. Search for **Gmail** → **Send an email**
3. To: your email address
4. Subject: `Social Post Draft — {{1.Topic}}`
5. Content: Click in the field, then map: HTTP module → body → content → 0 → text

**Test and Activate:**
1. Click **Run once**
2. Add a row to your Google Sheet with a topic (e.g., "The future of AI coding tools")
3. Watch the scenario execute — the flow turns green on each successful module
4. Check your inbox for the drafted social post
5. Click the clock icon to schedule: every 15 minutes (or any interval)
6. Toggle the scenario ON

**What to observe:** The HTTP module gives you direct access to any API Make doesn't have a native module for. This pattern works for any REST API — not just Anthropic.

## Make vs n8n vs Zapier: The Honest Comparison

| | Make | n8n | Zapier |
|--|------|-----|--------|
| Free tier AI | HTTP module only | Native AI nodes free | Paid plan required |
| Visual style | Circular canvas | Flowchart canvas | Step-by-step form |
| Best for | Visual thinkers, data transformation | Maximum power + free | Fastest setup |
| Claude native | No (use HTTP) | Yes | No (use Webhook or paid) |
| Complexity | Medium | Medium-high | Low |

None of these tools is objectively best — they're tradeoffs. Most people settle on one and learn it well.

sections.title: Workshop A — Make Scenario Exploration
sections.content:
Explore Make (formerly Integromat) and understand its visual approach.

**Step 1 — Log into Make** (make.com — free plan available).

**Step 2 — Explore the visual scenario builder.** How does it differ from Zapier's linear Zap model? Note that Make supports:
- Loops (iterate over arrays)
- Multiple branches/routes
- Error handlers at the module level
- Aggregators (combine multiple records)

**Step 3 — Ask Claude:** *"Compare Make's visual automation builder to Zapier for complex workflows. What specific capabilities does Make have that Zapier cannot do or does poorly? When would I choose Make over Zapier?"*

**Step 4 — Explore a template** from Make's template library for a workflow relevant to your work.

**Step 5 — Identify a workflow** that would be complex on Zapier but simpler on Make (involving loops, multiple data transformations, or non-linear branching).

sections.title: Workshop B — Build a Make Scenario with Data Transformation
sections.content:
Build a Make scenario that involves real data transformation — Make's strength.

**Step 1 — Choose a scenario** where you need to process multiple items:
- Fetch all GitHub issues, classify each with AI, save classified results to a spreadsheet
- Get a daily report CSV, transform each row, send personalised emails
- Process a list of URLs, extract content from each, summarise all and send a digest

**Step 2 — Ask Claude Code to design the Make scenario:**
```
I want to build this in Make (formerly Integromat):
[describe your scenario]

Help me:
1. Which modules should I use?
2. How should I structure the iterator/aggregator?
3. For the AI step, write the HTTP module configuration to call the Anthropic API
4. What's the data transformation approach at each step?
```

**Step 3 — Build the scenario** following Claude's design.

**Step 4 — Test with real data.** Verify the output for 3 input items.

**Step 5 — Mandatory review:** Ask: *"What failure modes exist in this scenario? What happens when the Anthropic API returns an unexpected format?"*

sections.title: Workshop C — Make Error Handling and Monitoring
sections.content:
Configure Make's error handling features.

**Step 1 — Ask Claude:** *"Explain Make's error handling approaches: error handlers, ignore, break, resume, rollback, commit. When should I use each?"*

**Step 2 — Add error handling to your scenario:**
- Add a Break handler to the HTTP module (stops iteration on that item, continues with others)
- Add a final error notification module

**Step 3 — Test error handling** by sending a malformed input that will cause the HTTP module to fail. Does the scenario handle it gracefully?

**Step 4 — Configure scenario monitoring:**
- Set up email notifications for scenario failures
- Configure Make's built-in scenario monitoring (if available on your plan)

**Step 5 — Ask Claude:** "Design a monitoring approach for a Make scenario that processes 500 records nightly. How would I know if 10% of records failed to process correctly?"

sections.title: Workshop D — Automation Consolidation Review
sections.content:
Review all the automation tools you've tried and consolidate your approach.

**Step 1 — List every automation you've built or tested** across Lessons 10-1 through 10-4: n8n, Zapier, Make.

**Step 2 — For each automation**, rate it:
- Does it work reliably? (1-5)
- Does it deliver real value? (1-5)
- Is it maintainable? (1-5)

**Step 3 — Ask Claude:** *"Based on these automations [describe them], which should I invest time in improving vs abandoning? What is the highest-value next automation I should build?"*

**Step 4 — Choose ONE tool** as your primary automation platform going forward (or define when you'd use each). Write a one-paragraph explanation of your choice.

**Step 5 — Commit to running at least one automation in production** for 30 days before evaluating whether to continue.

sections.question: Make's iterator module processes 100 items and 5 fail. What happens by default, and what should you configure instead?
options: The entire scenario fails if any item fails
By default, a failing item breaks the iterator; configure a Break error handler to skip failed items, continue with successful ones, and log failures separately
Make automatically retries failed items 3 times
Failed items are automatically added to a retry queue
sections.explanation: Make's default iterator behaviour on error can halt the entire batch. For scenarios processing multiple items where partial failure is acceptable, configure error handlers appropriately: Break (skip the failed item and continue), or Resume (mark as failed but continue). Also add a post-processing step to collect and report on failures. A scenario that successfully processes 95/100 items with a clear failure report is much more useful than one that stops at the first failure.

sections.question: Make charges per operation (module run). A scenario with 5 modules runs on 200 items. How many operations does this use?
options: 200 operations — per run of the scenario
5 operations — per module in the scenario
200 operations — the iterator counts as one
sections.explanation: Make counts per module execution, not per scenario run. If an iterator processes 200 items through 5 modules each: 200 × 5 = 1000 operations. This is critical for cost planning: a scenario that seems simple (5 modules) but processes large datasets becomes expensive at scale. Design Make scenarios to minimise modules in the inner loop (inside iterators) and use aggregators or bulk operations where possible.

sections.content: **You've completed lesson 10-4.** You've seen all three major no-code automation platforms and know how to call the Anthropic API from any of them, even without a native module. Next: using AI to improve your git workflows.
